rows.correction: The name of this integration entry in Home Assistant's list of integrations. It is not part of entity names: they all start with "Heat Pump Optimizer".

Required when source is entity; typical attrs raw_today/raw_tomorrow

Gap between target and minimum gives savings room
rows.why: the plan pulls toward the day/night comfort temperatures, so the savings room is their gap to the minimum, not the target's
rows.correction: How warm you want the house, and how far the optimizer may drift from that to save money. The gap between the comfort temperatures and the minimum is what makes savings possible: the wider it is, the more the house can coast through expensive hours.

rows.claim: Optimizer aims for target_temperature and only drifts to avoid expensive hours
rows.why: Per-step pull is get_comfort_temp (day/night/weekend/holiday); target_temp only caps stored-heat value, seeds baselines and the idle fallback, backs the climate entity, and must lie within min/max.
rows.correction: The house's reference temperature: the thermostat (climate) entity shows and sets it. The plan itself aims for the daytime and night-time comfort temperatures below and only drifts away from them to avoid expensive hours. It has to sit between the coldest and warmest acceptable temperatures.

rows.claim: Coldest the plan will take the house; soft but heavily priced
rows.why: Night floor is min-0.5, Economy and the open-window option widen it downward (floored at 15 °C), and the plan's gap is to the comfort temperatures, not the target.
rows.correction: The coldest the plan will take the house in the daytime; at night the limit is 0.5 K lower. The Economy optimization mode lowers it by a further 1.5 K, and a detected open window by 1 K when Ease heating while a window is open is on, never below 15 °C. A strongly priced bound rather than a hard constraint — a hard one would leave a cold morning the pump cannot heat through with no plan at all — but breaching it costs far more than the electricity saved, at prices a couple of orders of magnitude beyond real ones, so the plan holds above it. A wider gap to the comfort temperatures means more room to save.

rows.claim: Max is priced like the minimum and just as firm; plan aims for target
rows.why: Only 'aims for the target temperature' is false (the pull is to the day/night comfort temperatures); the half-weight overshoot penalty is a harmless difference at real prices so that sentence is kept.
rows.correction: The warmest the plan will pre-heat the house to during cheap hours. Priced the same way as the minimum, and just as firm at any real price. A limit, never a target: the plan aims for the daytime and night-time comfort temperatures and only comes near this when cheap hours make storing heat worth it. It cannot hold back heat the house gets for free, so a sunny summer room may still drift above it.

rows.claim: Last sentence: unit is a declaration; integration never recommends a space set-point (rest: unit semantics, 5 K return offset, 25 C gate)
rows.why: Only the last sentence is false: under Control the arbiter writes the plan's room (Indoor) or water (Flow/Return) temperature to the entity; the 5 K offset and 25/20 °C gates check out.
rows.correction: Indoor temperature is correct for a room or thermostat set-point. Flow temperature is for a controller whose set-point is a water temperature it holds its supply at. Return temperature is for a controller that takes the set-point as its return-water target (assumed for a Luxtronik through its Smart Home Interface); it is written like a flow set-point, with the rated hold, the weather curve and the 25 °C gate moved 5 K down to return terms. A version before this option reads Return temperature as Indoor temperature: switch it back to Flow temperature before downgrading. Pointing an indoor target at a flow entity would command roughly 21 °C to something expecting 35–45 °C and badly underheat the house. The unit tells the optimizer what the number means: with Pump duty control at Control it writes the plan's room temperature (Indoor temperature) or water temperature (Flow temperature, Return temperature) to this entity.

rows.claim: Learned offset capped at 15 C so only part of extra work priced; plus off by default, valve refusal, watch skips intervals without fresh supply reading
rows.why: FLOW_BIAS_CLAMP_K (15) bounds only the downward side; the upward bound is a 75 °C supply (FLOW_SUPPLY_MAX_C) minus the curve.
rows.correction: Off by default. For a system with no mixing valve, where the pump feeds the radiators or floor loops directly. When on, plans and costs account for the pump working harder to make hotter water: the supply temperature is taken from the model's own weather curve, plus the offset learned from the supply water temperature sensor if you have one. With that sensor, the efficiency health watch also judges the pump at a common water temperature, so a hotter supply is not reported as a failing compressor, and it skips any interval where the sensor has no fresh reading, so while that sensor is unavailable the watch does not judge space heating at all. The learned offset can lower the supply at most 15 K below the model's curve and can raise it at most to a 75 °C supply. Not available with a mixing valve, whose tank temperature already sets the price.

rows.correction: Off (the default) never writes the pump's operating mode or set-points. Observe writes none either and keeps a 24-hour ledger, in the diagnostics, of the duty each plan step asked for against what the pump did (from the power entity, the mode and the tank temperature). With any of the three, the heat pump on/off switch, if you have set one, is still switched by the plan. Control writes the operating mode above (hot water only on hot-water-only steps, heating only on space-heating-only steps, unchanged on idle steps; on a step that plans both, hot water only for the hot-water share of the step and then heating, a share under 5 minutes going to the other duty; Heating + DHW while a boost or an anti-legionella cycle calls for both, and whenever the plan is not in charge), the hot water set-point entity (the hot water set-point configured on the hot water page, or the anti-legionella temperature during a cycle) and the space set-point entity (for a flow set-point, a target that follows the planned power — the heating flow (55 °C, or the Heating flow ceiling) at full power, toward 5 °C (or the Minimum lift above the inlet water) above the first fresh reading of the heat-pump return, buffer tank, floor return or valve outlet (35 °C when none is configured) at the modulation floor — on steps that heat the house, 25 °C on steps that do not (20 °C for a Return temperature set-point, or the entity's own minimum if that is higher), and 35 °C or the weather curve, whichever is higher, when the plan is not in charge; for an indoor one, the planned room temperature). Where the mode offers no single-duty option, as on the GCHV Modbus package, the other duty's set-point is lowered instead: the hot water one to 30 °C, a flow set-point to the same 25 °C (20 °C for Return temperature), an indoor one to 5 °C, each never below the entity's own minimum. A hot-water-only stretch is capped at 90 minutes (30 below -10 °C outdoors), unless the room is already at its planned temperature. Where Capacity limited (night mode) is a switch and silent windows are scheduled, Control also holds that switch on inside a silent window and off outside one. While Optimizer active is on, any change to those entities the optimizer did not make is written back at once; turn Optimizer active off to change the pump by hand. A value the pump does not hold raises a warning and is sent again every 5 minutes.
